Arminian
är-mĭn´ĭ-an
n. and adj. (one holding the system of Jacobus Arminius, 1560–1609; conditional election and resistible grace)
From Arminius, the Latinised name of Jakob Hermanszoon, professor at Leiden, whose followers set out five articles in the Remonstrance of 1610 — whence Remonstrant, the older name.

Biblical Definition

Arminianism affirms conditional election (God chooses those He foresaw would believe), a universal atonement, prevenient grace that is genuinely resistible, and, in most forms, the possibility of falling from grace. Its texts are real and must be answered: “God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son: that whosoever believeth in him should not perish” (John 3:16); God “will have all men to be saved, and to come unto the knowledge of the truth” (1Ti 2:4); Christ is “the propitiation… for the sins of the whole world” (1Jn 2:2); “whom he did foreknow, he also did predestinate” (Rom 8:29). The Reformed reply turns on what foreknowledge means and on whom the all and the world denote.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines Arminian as one of a sect or party of Christians, so called from Arminius, who holds that God has not fixed the future state of mankind by an absolute unconditional decree, but determined to bestow salvation on those who believe and persevere.

ARMINIAN, n. One of a sect or party of Christians, so called from Arminius, or Harmensen, of Holland.

ARMINIAN, a. Pertaining to the Arminians. The distinguishing tenets are: that God has not fixed the future state of mankind by an absolute unconditional decree; that Jesus Christ died for all men and not for the elect only; that man has power to do good works; and that grace is not irresistible.

Key Scripture

John 3:16 — "For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life."

1Ti 2:4 — "Who will have all men to be saved, and to come unto the knowledge of the truth."

1Jn 2:2 — "And he is the propitiation for our sins: and not for ours only, but also for the sins of the whole world."

Rom 8:29 — "For whom he did foreknow, he also did predestinate to be conformed to the image of his Son, that he might be the firstborn among many brethren."

Rom 9:16 — "So then it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy."

Modern Corruption

The name is used as an insult for anyone insufficiently precise, and it names a definite historical system that deserves to be answered rather than sneered at.

expand to see more

The word has become the Reformed world's general-purpose slur, applied to any believer who has not read Dort — which is most of the church, including a great many who would accept the doctrines of grace if anyone put them kindly. That usage is both uncharitable and imprecise. Arminianism is a defined system, set out in five articles in 1610 by men who were pastors and scholars, and it was answered article by article at Dort in a document that took months. A position worth a synod is worth an argument, and the man who can only produce the label has not made one.

The genuine difference is not over whether faith is required — both sides say it is — but over where faith comes from. The Reformed hold that it is the gift of God (Eph 2:8) and the fruit of a new birth that precedes it (John 1:13); the Arminian holds that prevenient grace restores the ability and the man decides. Everything else follows from that one question, including whether the decisive difference between the saved and the lost lies finally in God or in the man; and every honest conversation about the five points arrives there sooner or later.

The Reformed should also concede what the texts plainly say. God does declare that He has no pleasure in the death of the wicked; the offer of the gospel is universal, sincere, and to be pressed on every creature; and a hyper-Calvinism that will not freely invite sinners has departed further from Scripture than the Arminianism it despises. Ezekiel 33:11 and Romans 9:16 are both in the book, and a theology that can only hold one of them is not yet finished.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek proginosko (G4267), to foreknow; pas (G3956), all; kosmos (G2889), world; thelo (G2309), to will, desire.

expand to see more

Greek proginosko (G4267) — to foreknow; Romans 8:29, 11:2, 1 Peter 1:20 — of persons, not of facts about them.

Greek kosmos (G2889) — world; John 3:16, 1 John 2:2, and of the ordered system opposed to God, 1 John 2:15.

Greek thelo (G2309) — to will, desire; 1 Timothy 2:4, 2 Peter 3:9, Matthew 23:37.

Usage

"“Whom he did foreknow, he also did predestinate” — the verse the whole debate turns on."

"“Who will have all men to be saved” — a text the Reformed must answer, not avoid."

"“Not of him that willeth… but of God” — the answer, and it is a text too."
